questions.question: What is a package manager in Linux and why is it better than downloading software manually?
questions.answer: A package manager is a tool that automates installing, updating, and removing software by communicating with trusted repositories. It automatically resolves all dependencies, verifies package integrity via GPG signatures, and enables one-command installation. It is far superior to manual downloads because it handles dependencies automatically, ensures software comes from verified sources, and makes future updates trivial.

questions.question: What is a Linux repository?
questions.answer: A repository is a central, trusted storage location of verified software packages. Linux distributions (like Amazon Linux or Ubuntu) configure their systems to pull packages from these repositories. Packages in official repos are tested, GPG-signed, and maintained by the distribution owner (Amazon for Amazon Linux, Canonical for Ubuntu). Repository configuration files on Amazon Linux are stored in /etc/yum.repos.d/.

questions.question: What is the difference between YUM and APT?
questions.answer: Both are package managers but for different Linux distributions. YUM (Yellowdog Updater, Modified) is used on Amazon Linux, Red Hat, CentOS, and Fedora — it works with .rpm package files. APT (Advanced Package Tool) is used on Ubuntu and Debian — it works with .deb package files. For AWS EC2 running Amazon Linux, YUM is the default package manager.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'yum update' and 'yum upgrade'?
questions.answer: 'yum update' refreshes the local repository metadata — it tells the system which versions of software are currently available in the repositories, but does NOT install anything. 'yum upgrade' actually downloads and installs newer versions of all installed packages. You must always run 'yum update' first to get fresh metadata, then 'yum upgrade' to use that metadata to update software.

questions.question: What is OS patching and why is it critical for servers?
questions.answer: OS patching means applying small code updates to fix or improve existing software without replacing it completely. It is critical because: (1) it fixes security vulnerabilities that hackers exploit on unpatched servers, (2) it resolves software bugs that cause errors, (3) it improves performance, and (4) it adds minor feature enhancements. On Linux, unlike Windows, patches do not push pop-up notifications — admins must check and apply manually or automate the process.

questions.question: What are the three tiers of a 3-tier web application?
questions.answer: (1) Frontend (Tier 1): What users see and interact with in their browser. Served by web server software like Apache or Nginx. Handles HTTP requests and delivers HTML/CSS/JS files. (2) Backend (Tier 2): The business logic layer. Runs on Node.js, Flask, or similar frameworks. Processes user requests, validates data, and queries the database. (3) Database (Tier 3): Stores all persistent data. Runs on MySQL, PostgreSQL, etc. Responds to queries from the backend.

questions.question: What does a Linux software package contain?
questions.answer: A Linux package is a compressed bundle containing four components: (1) Program files — the actual executables and libraries, (2) Dependencies — declarations of other software this package requires, (3) Configuration files — default settings placed in /etc/, and (4) Metadata — information about the package including name, version, license, and description. After installation, files are placed in standard system directories: executables in /usr/bin/, configs in /etc/, libraries in /usr/lib/.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the -y flag in 'sudo yum install git -y'?
questions.answer: The -y flag tells YUM to automatically answer 'yes' to all confirmation prompts during installation. Without -y, YUM stops and asks 'Is this ok [y/d/N]?' before downloading. With -y, it proceeds without waiting for input — essential for automation scripts, CI/CD pipelines, and any non-interactive installation scenario.

questions.question: How do you check if a software package is installed on Amazon Linux?
questions.answer: Two ways: (1) Use the application's version command: git --version or python3 --version — if installed, shows version; if not, shows 'command not found'. (2) Use YUM info: yum info git — shows whether the package is installed or just available in the repository, along with complete version and repository details.

questions.question: What are the three types of software in Linux and give examples of each?
questions.answer: (1) System Software: Core programs that run and manage the OS — examples: Linux kernel, bash shell, systemd. Cannot function without these. (2) Application Software: End-user or service-facing programs — examples: Apache, Nginx, MySQL, Git, Python. Installed based on server purpose. (3) Utility Software: Supporting helper tools — examples: vim (text editor), chmod (permissions), ls (list files), tar (compression). Used for system administration.

questions.question: Walk me through deploying a frontend web application on a fresh Amazon Linux EC2 instance from scratch.
questions.answer: (Situation) New EC2 instance with no software installed. (Task) Deploy a frontend HTML app accessible via browser. (Action) SSH into the instance. Run 'sudo yum update -y' to refresh repos. Run 'sudo yum install httpd -y' to install Apache. Run 'sudo systemctl start httpd' and 'sudo systemctl enable httpd' to start and persist the service. Create the HTML file in /var/www/html/index.html. Open port 80 in the EC2 security group. (Result) Navigate to the EC2 public IP in a browser — the application loads successfully.

questions.question: A production server running a Node.js application needs security patches. How would you approach this safely?
questions.answer: (Situation) Production server needs patches but runs an active application. (Task) Apply security patches without causing downtime or breaking the app. (Action) First, 'sudo yum check-update' to review what updates are available. Review the update list — identify if any packages could conflict with Node.js dependencies. Communicate the maintenance window to the team. Test the same patch on a staging server first. After confirmation, apply targeted patches: 'sudo yum update <specific-package> -y' rather than a blanket upgrade. Verify the application still runs correctly after patching. (Result) Security vulnerability addressed with zero application downtime.

questions.question: A user reports they can open the company website but cannot log in. Which tier do you investigate first?
questions.answer: (Situation) Website loads correctly but authentication fails. (Task) Identify which of the three tiers has the issue. (Action) Since the page loads (frontend/Tier 1 is working), the issue is either in Tier 2 (backend processing the login) or Tier 3 (database storing credentials). Check backend application logs first — look for authentication errors or database connection failures. Then check database connectivity. (Result) By eliminating the frontend and narrowing to backend/database, the root cause is found faster.

questions.question: You need to install three packages — git, python3, and nginx — on a new EC2 instance as part of a startup script. Write the commands.
questions.answer: (Situation) Automating server setup via a shell script. (Task) Install multiple packages non-interactively. (Action) The complete startup commands would be: sudo yum update -y (refresh repo metadata) then sudo yum install git python3 nginx -y (install all three in one transaction with auto-yes). Adding -y is critical for non-interactive scripts. After installation, verify with: git --version && python3 --version && nginx -v. (Result) All three packages installed in two commands with no manual prompts required.

questions.question: A team member says 'I can't find the config file for Apache anywhere.' How do you help them?
questions.answer: (Situation) Team member is new to Linux and unfamiliar with file locations. (Task) Explain where configuration files live after package installation. (Action) Explain that after installing any RPM package, configuration files are placed in /etc/ — so Apache's main config is at /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf. You can also use 'yum info httpd' to see package details, or 'rpm -ql httpd' to list every file installed by the httpd package and their locations. (Result) Team member understands the Linux filesystem hierarchy and knows where to look for any package's configuration.

questions.question: How would you automate OS patch checks on a fleet of Linux servers so that admins are notified when updates are available?
questions.answer: (Situation) Managing 20+ EC2 instances that need regular patch monitoring. (Task) Automate update checks without manually SSH-ing into each server. (Action) Two approaches: (1) Script-based — write a shell script that runs 'yum check-update' and emails results, scheduled via cron. (2) AWS-native — use AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager with a maintenance window and compliance reporting. This scales to hundreds of instances, provides dashboards, and integrates with SNS for notifications. (Result) No manual server logins needed — automated detection and optional automated remediation.

questions.question: What happens step by step when you run 'sudo yum install git -y' on Amazon Linux?
questions.answer: (Situation) Fresh server, git not installed. (Task) Understand the internal flow of package installation. (Action) (1) YUM reads /etc/yum.repos.d/ to find configured repositories. (2) YUM queries the repository metadata to locate the git package. (3) YUM reads git's dependency list and checks what's already installed. (4) YUM presents the download plan (8 packages, 7.9MB). With -y, proceeds automatically. (5) Packages are downloaded and GPG signatures verified. (6) Packages are installed in dependency order. (7) YUM updates the local RPM database at /var/lib/rpm/. (Result) git is installed and 'git --version' confirms success.

questions.question: A developer complains that after 'sudo yum upgrade -y', their Python Flask application stopped working. What likely happened?
questions.answer: (Situation) Application broke after a blanket system upgrade. (Task) Diagnose the root cause. (Action) The most likely cause is a Python version upgrade — Flask depends on specific Python versions and their associated library APIs. Check 'python3 --version' to see the new version. Review Flask logs for import errors or API compatibility issues. The fix: either upgrade the application code to be compatible with the new Python version, or pin the Python version in the repo configuration to prevent future auto-upgrades. (Result) This is why 'yum upgrade' in production always requires team review — version changes can silently break applications.

questions.question: Explain the security advantage of using repositories over downloading software from the internet.
questions.answer: (Situation) Choosing between installing via YUM repository vs. downloading from a vendor website. (Task) Justify the security preference for repositories. (Action) Repositories provide: (1) GPG signature verification — every package is cryptographically signed; YUM rejects unsigned or tampered packages. (2) Central trust model — you trust one source (Amazon/Canonical) rather than individually vetting dozens of vendor sites. (3) Integrity checking — package checksums are verified on download. (4) No phishing risk — no risk of downloading from a fake website. Repositories are the Linux security gold standard for software installation. (Result) Repository-based installation eliminates entire categories of software supply chain attacks.

questions.question: A new EC2 server is created every time the application scales out. How should software installation be handled on these ephemeral servers?
questions.answer: (Situation) Auto Scaling creates new EC2 instances on demand — each needs identical software setup. (Task) Automate consistent software installation across dynamically created instances. (Action) Use EC2 User Data (startup script) to run installation commands when the instance first launches: sudo yum update -y, then install required packages. Alternatively, use a pre-baked AMI (Amazon Machine Image) that already has software installed — faster startup. For complex setups, use AWS Systems Manager State Manager or a configuration management tool to enforce desired software state. (Result) Every new instance has identical, verified software without manual intervention.

questions.question: Design the software stack for a scalable e-commerce application on AWS EC2 running Amazon Linux. List each tier, the software required, and the YUM install commands.
questions.answer: Frontend Tier: Install Nginx (sudo yum install nginx -y) to serve the React/HTML/CSS frontend. Start with systemctl start nginx. Configuration at /etc/nginx/nginx.conf. Backend Tier: Install Node.js or Python (sudo yum install nodejs -y or sudo yum install python3 -y) for the Express/Flask application server. This handles API requests from the frontend and business logic. Database Tier: Install MySQL (sudo yum install mysql-server -y) for relational data storage. In production, prefer Amazon RDS over self-managed MySQL for managed backups, multi-AZ, and automatic patching. Architecture note: Use separate EC2 instances for each tier for independent scaling, not all tiers on one machine.

questions.question: What is the difference between a package manager removing a package vs. simply deleting its files?
questions.answer: Using 'sudo yum remove git' properly removes the package by: uninstalling all git files from their system directories, updating the RPM database (/var/lib/rpm/) to reflect git is no longer installed, optionally removing dependencies that were installed solely for git. Simply deleting files (rm -rf /usr/bin/git) leaves the RPM database believing git is still installed, orphans other installed files from the git package, and leaves dependencies that are no longer needed. Always use the package manager for removal to maintain system consistency.

questions.question: How would you securely add a third-party YUM repository (like Docker's official repo) to an Amazon Linux server?
questions.answer: (1) Obtain the official .repo file or repository URL from the vendor's official documentation — never from third-party sources. (2) Verify the GPG key fingerprint matches the vendor's published key. (3) Add the .repo file to /etc/yum.repos.d/ or use 'yum-config-manager --add-repo <url>'. (4) Import the vendor's GPG key: sudo rpm --import <gpg-key-url>. (5) Run 'sudo yum update -y' to refresh metadata including the new repo. (6) Install the package: 'sudo yum install docker -y'. YUM will verify package signatures against the imported GPG key on every install from that repo.

questions.question: Why is 'yum update' (metadata refresh) a separate operation from 'yum upgrade' (package update) rather than one combined operation?
questions.answer: Separating them provides critical control: (1) You can see what's available before committing to any changes. (2) You can run 'yum check-update' after updating metadata to review pending changes before applying them. (3) In CI/CD pipelines, you can update metadata at build start and selectively upgrade only specific packages rather than everything. (4) On slow networks, caching fresh metadata separately avoids redownloading it for multiple subsequent operations. The separation reflects Linux's philosophy of predictable, composable commands — each doing one thing.

questions.question: How does AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager differ from manual yum patching, and when would you choose each?
questions.answer: Manual yum patching (ssh → yum update → yum upgrade) is appropriate for: single servers, learning/testing, specific one-off patches. AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager is appropriate for: fleets of 10+ EC2 instances, automated maintenance windows, compliance reporting, patching without SSH access, audit trails for security teams. Patch Manager lets you define patch baselines (which patches are approved), target groups of instances by tag, schedule patching during maintenance windows, and generate compliance dashboards. It eliminates the need to manually SSH into each instance and provides a single control plane for all patching operations.
